01What's covered

What a service covers.

Routine servicing, plus the jobs that get put off until something goes bang at the ramp. The numbers match the drawing above.

Service sheet

Motor
Hours
Date
  1. 1

    Outboard servicing

    Oils, filters, plugs and a proper look over the whole motor, matched to the engine and the hours it has done.

  2. 2

    Gearbox oil & impellers

    Fresh gearbox oil, checked for water, and a new water pump impeller before the old one lets go and the motor overheats.

  3. 3

    Fuel filters, lines & bulbs

    Filters changed and perished lines, bulbs and clamps replaced, because stale or dirty fuel is behind a lot of breakdowns.

  4. 4

    Anodes, plugs & thermostats

    The small sacrificial and wear parts that are cheap to replace on time and expensive to ignore.

  5. 5

    Steering & control cables

    Stiff steering and a sticky throttle or gear shift sorted before a cable seizes or snaps.

02Service rhythm

How often it's due.

An outboard that lives in salt water needs looking after on a schedule, whether or not it has done many hours.

  1. You

    Every trip

    Flush the motor with fresh water, check the telltale is running strong, and look for oil or fishing line around the prop.

  2. The service

    100 hours or once a year, whichever comes first

    Oils, filters, plugs, gearbox oil and anodes, plus a check of everything that moves.

  3. The bigger items

    Every few seasons

    Water pump impeller, thermostat and fuel lines, sooner if the boat works hard or sits for long stretches.

Intervals vary from motor to motor. Your owner's manual has the schedule for yours, and we work to that.

03Don't wait for the date

Signs it's due now.

Most outboard trouble gives some warning first. Catching it at a service costs far less than finding it out on the water.

Book a service
  • 01Hard starting, rough idle or stalling
  • 02The overheat alarm, or a weak telltale stream
  • 03Milky gearbox oil, or oil around the prop
  • 04Steering or throttle getting stiff
  • 05A fuel smell, or a primer bulb that won't go firm
  • 06It has sat unused for most of a year

04Good to know

Servicing questions.

Can't see yours here? Ask it in the booking form or give us a call.

How often should an outboard be serviced?

Most manufacturers say every 100 hours or once a year, whichever comes first. Boats used in salt water, or left sitting for long stretches, do best on the yearly service even when the hours are low. Your owner's manual has the schedule for your motor.

Which outboards do you service?

Most of the common brands. Put the make, model and year in the booking form and we will confirm before you book it in.

What should I tell you when I book?

The make, model and year of the motor, roughly how many hours it has done, when it was last serviced and anything it has been doing that seems off. Photos or a short video help a lot.

Can you check the trailer at the same time?

Yes. Bearings, brakes and lights can be checked in the same booking, and it usually makes sense to do both together.
